2026 Paris Motor Show • Hyundai Tucson N Line Steals the Spotlight in Paris, but It's All Show and No Go
Elon Musk Wants Tesla To Double Its Production Capacity by 2030, Does This Even Make Sense?
7 photos
Photo: Tesla
For years, Elon Musk insisted that Tesla is no longer a carmaker, but an AI and robotics company. This coincided with EV sales plummeting in 2024 and 2025, which prompted Musk to pivot Tesla's strategy. However, Tesla sales miraculously rebounded in 2026, and not only is Tesla a carmaker again, but Musk wants to double production capacity. What gives?
Tesla held its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, after releasing some mixed financial results that split investors and analysts. Unlike the shareholder deck, the conference allowed Tesla to present a clearer picture of its operations. As is often the case, Tesla tried to dazzle investors with rosy prospects, and in many ways, it succeeded.
However, another part of the call raised serious questions: Elon Musk announced that Tesla aims to double production capacity to 5 million vehicles per year. And he wants to do it fast, by the end of 2030. This marks an abrupt change of direction after years of turning his back on vehicle manufacturing. We've read and heard the "Tesla is not a carmaker" mantra many times, but now things appear to move in the opposite direction.
From sustainable transport and energy to "amazing abundance" Over the past three years, Tesla went from plans to save the Earth with sustainable transportation, solar panels, and energy storage, to a fuzzy concept of "amazing abundance" that not even Musk can explain what it means exactly. Since then, the affordable Gen-3 compact EV was canceled, and the Model S and Model X were retired without successors. Instead, Tesla insisted that autonomous vehicles and robots are the company's future.
Many mocked Tesla's new ethos as a taxi company, but we have to give it credit for its Robotaxi service. What started as a pilot has since been expanded into a dependable transportation service in Austin using unsupervised vehicles. The Cybercab, which recently started volume production, has increased its presence, while safety records have proved that its autonomous driving system is at least as safe as Waymo's.
Meanwhile, nobody believed that Tesla would put much effort into expanding its EV portfolio. It never was the kind of traditional carmaker committed to regularly overhauling its model lineup. The Model 3 and Model Y were the only ones to receive meaningful updates, and that's not counting the stripped-down Standard variants. With the Cybertruck program in shambles and no new vehicle plans in the pipeline, Tesla looked set to abandon its automotive plans.
And don't even get me started on the Roadster, which was merely a PR stunt with little practical value. Even if Tesla finds a way and a time to start building it, it will be a small series model for collectors rather than a new vehicle line. However, there's some merit in the Roadster, beyond its qualities as a driver's car. Specifically, it's the only thing that made Musk reconsider cars.
From no new models to doubling the vehicle production There might be no connection between the Roadster's epic demo and the decision to double Tesla vehicle production capacity. However, given that Musk made the announcement roughly one week after watching the Roadster flying and rolling in the air, I believe that the October 15 event influenced him somehow. Maybe (he might have thought) cars can be cool after all.
Regardless of what made Musk change his mind , we now have this new announcement to make sense of. "We've been laying the groundwork for a lot more manufacturing capacity," Musk told investors at the earnings call. "We're aiming for 5 million vehicles a year by 2030." Now that's indeed a strong statement from a company that didn't want to talk about new car models not long ago.
Tesla already has more production capacity than it can use. According to Tesla's latest data, it can theoretically build 1,5 million Model 3 and Model Y vehicles in Fremont and Shanghai, plus another 750.000 Model Y vehicles across Austin and Berlin. That's a 2.25-million annual capacity for the two popular EVs plus 125,000 Cybertrucks and 125,000 Cybercabs. Tesla Semi accounts for an additional 25,000-unit capacity.
Meanwhile, Tesla sales maxed out at 1.8 million in 2023, and it's not yet clear if it could match that performance in 2026. Why does Tesla need twice the production capacity, and why so fast, by the end of 2030? Why does Musk expect Tesla to triple its vehicle sales in just four years? Does Musk really think that Cybercab production could reach the 2-million-unit level he promised in 2023? Or does it have other mass-market models in the pipeline that he expects to require a production capacity increase?
Two million Cybercabs or new mass-market models? If we're to consider what Musk told investors during the third-quarter earnings call , he believes that Tesla could've sold more vehicles in the quarter. Musk blamed tight battery supply for not being able to increase production. Certainly, the EV sales boom caused by high fuel prices could hardly be anticipated. It's obvious that Tesla was caught off-guard by the strong demand, especially in China and Europe.
However, going from selling "more" to selling three times as many vehicles is a long stretch. When Tesla launched Cybercab's production, Musk was confident that it could sell 2 million units per year. However, that's almost incomprehensible, considering the lack of customer appeal of a car with no controls and only two seats.
During the call, Musk announced that Tesla would sell the first Cybercab units to customers later this year. However, he also admitted that these customers would be fleet operators, not private owners. Musk also said that the vast majority of Cybercabs would be owned by Tesla, so, again, no private customers. Does Tesla need 2 million new Cybercabs every year for its own operations? That's a question that's worth a lot of money.
The only other possibility is that Tesla reconsidered its previous position and is now working on new vehicle models. If that's true, it could start with the affordable compact EV that shares the unboxed Gen-3 platform with the Cybercab. That would be the easiest and cheapest route to doubling production. Certainly, more new mass-market models would help fill that 5-million annual capacity much faster.
